subsection: 6. Electoral reform, sectarianism in politics, Fenianism and Liberal reforms, 1850–1870

notes.h: Electoral reform and the Irish franchise
notes.b: The franchise (the right to vote) decided how much weight tenant farmers could have in politics. Between 1829 and 1850 the Irish electorate was cut, nudged up and then widened in the counties, but voting stayed open and landlords and clergy could still lean on voters.
points: Alongside the Catholic Emancipation Act of 1829, which let Catholics sit as MPs, a second Act (the Disenfranchisement Act) abolished the forty-shilling freeholders, the small landholders who had voted, and raised the county qualification to £10 freeholders. The Irish county electorate fell sharply, by a very large proportion.

The Irish Reform Act of 1832 raised the number of Irish seats in the Westminster Parliament, which Irish MPs had joined after the Act of Union (1800), from 100 to 105. It gave the borough vote to £10 householders, but the electorate stayed small beside Britain's.

Voting was open, not secret, until the Ballot Act of 1872 introduced secret voting. Until then landlords, agents and priests could see how people voted and pressure tenants and parishioners, which is why a bigger electorate did not mean a free one.

The Irish Franchise Act of 1850 gave the county vote to occupiers rated at £12 or more and the borough vote to occupiers rated at £8 or more. Being 'rated' means the property was valued for local tax.
The 1850 Act made a big difference in the counties, where the electorate more than doubled, because many tenant farmers now qualified. The borough electorate remained small.

A larger county electorate of tenant farmers helped Tenant League candidates do well at the general election of 1852. Even so, the Famine (1845-50), emigration and eviction had already thinned out the small tenants, so the new voters were a smaller class than before.
notes.tip: Keep the three franchise measures apart: 1829 (Disenfranchisement Act, forty-shilling freeholders abolished), 1832 (Reform Act, seats 100 to 105) and 1850 (Franchise Act, £12 county and £8 borough). Say the 1850 county electorate 'more than doubled' rather than quoting figures.

notes.h: Sectarianism in politics: the Orange Order and Dolly's Brae
notes.b: Sectarianism, hostility between Catholic and Protestant communities that shapes politics, ran through Irish public life at the end of the 1840s. Orange marches were the most visible sign, and Dolly's Brae showed how quickly they could turn violent.
points: The Orange Order was founded in 1795 near Loughgall, County Armagh, after the Battle of the Diamond, a clash between Protestant and Catholic groups in September 1795. It aimed to defend the Protestant ascendancy (the dominant position of Protestants in Irish life) and the link with Britain.

The Order was dissolved in 1836 after a parliamentary inquiry into its spread in the army, so it lost its formal organisation. It was revived in Ulster in the 1840s, which is why Orange marches were a live issue by 1849.

On 12 July 1849 an Orange procession returning from Lord Roden's estate at Tollymore passed through Dolly's Brae, near Castlewellan, County Down. Armed Catholics, known as Ribbonmen (members of a secret agrarian and Catholic society), had gathered there.
Fighting followed and Catholics were killed, though the number is disputed because estimates vary widely. Catholic houses nearby were burned.
An inquiry criticised the Orangemen and Lord Roden, and he lost his place on the commission of the peace (the body of local magistrates).
The Party Processions Act (1850) banned party processions, such as Orange and Catholic marches, in an attempt to stop clashes like Dolly's Brae. It was repealed in 1872.
notes.tip: Dolly's Brae is a date-and-detail question: 12 July 1849, Orange march from Tollymore, armed Ribbonmen, Catholics killed, houses burned. Don't give a death toll; say the number is disputed.

notes.h: Sectarianism in politics: the Ecclesiastical Titles Act (1851)
notes.b: Sectarian feeling also came from Britain. A decision by the Pope in 1850 provoked a British law that Irish Catholics saw as an insult, and it drew them closer to tenant-right politics.
points: In September 1850 Pope Pius IX restored the Catholic hierarchy in England with territorial titles (bishops named after English places), making Wiseman archbishop of Westminster. Lord John Russell, the Whig prime minister, condemned this as papal aggression, a phrase widely used by the press and his supporters.

The Ecclesiastical Titles Act (1851) banned Catholic bishops from taking territorial titles in the United Kingdom. It was never enforced, so it achieved little except anger, and it was repealed in 1871.
Irish Catholic MPs opposed the Act, and the Catholic Defence Association was formed in 1851 to resist it. This pushed Catholic politics and tenant-right politics together.
Do not confuse this Act with the Irish Church Act of 1869. The Titles Act (1851) dealt with Catholic bishops' titles, while the 1869 Act disestablished the Church of Ireland.
notes.tip: Examiners reward getting the sequence right: papal restoration (1850), Russell's reaction, the Act (1851, never enforced, repealed 1871), then the Irish response. Don't mix it up with the 1869 Church Act.

notes.h: The Tenant League and the Independent Irish Party
notes.b: A new alliance of tenant-right campaigners and Catholic MPs promised independent opposition in the 1850s. Then it collapsed when two of its leading MPs took government jobs.
points: The Irish Tenant League was founded in Dublin in 1850 by Charles Gavan Duffy, Frederick Lucas, a Catholic convert and editor of the Tablet, and others, with support from Presbyterian ministers in Ulster. Its Ulster backers show it was not only a Catholic movement.

It demanded fair rent, fixity of tenure (the right not to be evicted while paying rent) and free sale of the tenant's interest (the right to sell the tenancy). The label 'the three Fs' became common only later.

Archbishop John MacHale of Tuam and Fr Patrick Lavelle supported the League, but the clergy were not united, so its backing was limited. Cardinal Cullen and many bishops distrusted priests in politics.

At the 1852 general election more than 40 MPs were returned pledged to independent opposition (refusing office from any government that did not meet tenant demands). They formed the Independent Irish Party.

In December 1852 William Keogh became solicitor-general for Ireland (a law officer of the government) and John Sadleir a Lord of the Treasury in Lord Aberdeen's government. This broke the pledge of independence.
Duffy, Lucas and others denounced them as betrayers because they had broken the pledge, so the party fractured as members drifted to the Liberals.
Lucas died in 1855 and Duffy emigrated to Australia in 1855, ending the movement. Sadleir, a financier, died by suicide in 1856 after the Tipperary Bank collapsed, and Keogh became a judge.
Many nationalists lost faith in parliamentary action because the party's own MPs had sold out, which helped turn young men towards Fenianism.
notes.tip: Don't confuse Frederick Lucas (Tenant League, died 1855) with Thomas Clarke Luby (Fenian), or Sadleir (financier, suicide) with Keogh (became a judge). Keep to the 1850 League, not the Land League of 1879.

notes.b: Fenianism was a transatlantic revolutionary movement that aimed to end British rule by force and set up an Irish republic. It grew from the disappointments of the 1840s and 1850s, and its creed is known as physical force republicanism.
points: Physical force republicanism is the belief that Ireland could win independence as a republic only by armed rebellion. Fenianism (the movement of the IRB and the Fenian Brotherhood) was its main expression in this period.

The Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB) was founded in Dublin on 17 March 1858 by James Stephens, with Thomas Clarke Luby and others, as an oath-bound secret society. The oath and secrecy were meant to protect members from informers.

In New York in the same year John O'Mahony founded the Fenian Brotherhood, which raised money and men in the United States. Its name came from the Fianna, the legendary warrior bands of Irish tradition. 'Fenians' covers both organisations.

The roots of Fenianism lay in the failed 1848 rising, bitterness left by the Famine, disillusion with parliamentary politics after the Independent Irish Party, and the experience of emigrants in exile.

The IRB was organised in circles under local leaders and reported to Stephens, who took the title of Chief Organiser of the Irish Republic. Members were mainly artisans (skilled workers), clerks, shopkeepers and farmers' sons, and the IRB tried to recruit soldiers in the British army.

The funeral of Terence Bellew MacManus, a 1848 rebel who died in California, drew a very large crowd in Dublin in November 1861 and showed Fenian strength. Cardinal Cullen refused to let his body lie in the Pro-Cathedral.
The movement's newspaper, the Irish People, began in Dublin in 1863, with Luby, John O'Leary and Charles Kickham as editors and Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa as manager.
American Fenians included many veterans of the American Civil War (1861-65), whose military experience raised hopes that a rising in Ireland could succeed.
notes.tip: Keep the two bodies apart: the IRB (Ireland, Stephens, Dublin, 17 March 1858) and the Fenian Brotherhood (USA, O'Mahony, New York). For Ordinary Level, learn the IRB's founding date, the oath, its members and its recruitment of soldiers.

notes.b: The government struck at the Irish organisation before it was ready. The rising Stephens had promised was delayed, his followers removed him, and when it came in 1867 it was quickly crushed.
points: In September 1865 the police raided the offices of the Irish People and arrested Luby, O'Leary, Rossa and Kickham. In November Stephens himself was arrested.
Stephens escaped from Richmond Prison in Dublin in November 1865 with the help of warders and fellow Fenians, and went abroad.
Habeas corpus (the right not to be held without trial) was suspended in Ireland in February 1866, allowing arrest without trial and making it easier to round up suspected Fenians.
In 1866 Stephens was in the United States, where he postponed the rising he had promised. His own followers deposed him in December 1866.
The rising took place in early March 1867 in snow and bad weather. Small risings in Dublin (Tallaght), Cork, Limerick and Tipperary were crushed within days.
Informers had compromised the plans, and the Fenians lacked arms and trained leaders, so the rising had little chance once the government knew what was coming.
notes.tip: For the 'why did the 1867 rising fail' question, give causes with a short reason each: informers, shortage of arms and leaders, bad weather, and the loss of leaders after the 1865 arrests.

notes.h: Fenian actions abroad and the Church's opposition
notes.b: Even after 1867 failed in Ireland, Fenian actions in England and Canada kept the movement in the public eye. They also showed its transatlantic reach and cost it sympathy in Britain.
points: On 18 September 1867 in Manchester, Fenians freed two prisoners, Thomas Kelly and Timothy Deasy, from a prison van, and a police sergeant, Charles Brett, was shot dead.

Three men, William Allen, Michael Larkin and Michael O'Brien, were hanged in Manchester on 23 November 1867 for Brett's death. They became known as the Manchester Martyrs and were mourned across Ireland, while Kelly and Deasy escaped.

On 13 December 1867 a Fenian bomb blew a hole in the wall of Clerkenwell prison in London in an attempt to free a prisoner. About a dozen people in the street nearby were killed, which turned British opinion against the Fenians.
Michael Barrett was hanged for Clerkenwell in 1868, the last public execution in England, so the affair ended a long tradition.
American Fenians raided Canada from the United States, at Ridgeway in June 1866 and again in 1870. Both raids failed to win Canadian territory, but they show the movement's international dimension.

Cardinal Cullen and most bishops condemned Fenianism as a secret society (the Church forbade oath-bound societies), and many priests denounced it from the altar. This cut Fenian support among devout Catholics.
notes.tip: Don't mix up Manchester (September 1867, rescue, Brett killed, Martyrs hanged in November) and Clerkenwell (London, December 1867, bomb). For the international dimension, say what each event shows: transatlantic reach, and what it cost, lost sympathy in Britain after Clerkenwell.

notes.b: Stephens founded and led the IRB and built the first lasting revolutionary organisation. His leadership failed at the decisive moment, when the promised rising did not come.
points: Born in Kilkenny in 1825, he took part in the 1848 rising at Ballingarry under William Smith O'Brien, where he was wounded, and escaped to Paris. Ballingarry gave him both his revolutionary experience and his sense that the next attempt needed better organisation.
He returned to Ireland in 1856 and travelled the country, then founded the IRB in 1858 as its Chief Organiser.
He worked with O'Mahony's Fenian Brotherhood in America, which sent money and supporters to Ireland, so the IRB had resources it could not raise at home.
He organised the Irish People in 1863 and built a network through secret circles, including recruitment in the British army.
He was arrested in November 1865 and escaped from Richmond Prison within a fortnight. In 1866 he was in the United States and failed to deliver the rising he had promised.
His own followers deposed him in December 1866, and he spent most of the rest of his life abroad, mainly in Paris. He returned to Ireland in 1891 and died in Dublin in 1901.
Contemporaries saw him as a gifted organiser and a charismatic figure, but also as autocratic (ruling without consulting others), secretive and over-promising.
Historians credit him with building the first lasting revolutionary organisation, while criticising his indecision and his failure to lead the rising he had promised.
notes.tip: Stephens essays need dates, deeds, how others saw him and how historians judge him. Learn the sequence: born 1825, Ballingarry 1848, return 1856, IRB 1858, Irish People 1863, arrest and escape 1865, deposed 1866. Don't mix him up with Kickham.

notes.b: Kickham combined Fenian leadership with literature. He was a writer and editor more than a conspirator, and he paid for his role with prison.
points: Born in Mullinahone, County Tipperary, in 1828, he was left almost deaf and with poor sight by a gunpowder accident in boyhood. This made him an unlikely soldier, so his contribution was in writing and ideas.
He wrote for The Nation, the Young Ireland newspaper, and joined the Fenians, becoming one of the editors of the Irish People.
Arrested in 1865, he was sentenced in 1866 to fourteen years' penal servitude (imprisonment with hard labour). He was released in 1869 on grounds of ill health.
He wrote the novel Sally Cavanagh (1869), about the eviction of a tenant family, and Knocknagow, or The Homes of Tipperary (1873), his most popular novel.
He became a prominent member of the IRB's Supreme Council (its governing body) in the 1870s and died at Blackrock, County Dublin, in 1882.
A practising Catholic, he was caught between his faith and the bishops' condemnation of the movement, and he rejected the clerical condemnation.
Contemporaries admired his courage, honesty and endurance in prison, which won respect even from people who disliked Fenianism.
Historians see him as the voice of rural, literary Fenianism, the link between nationalism and literature.
notes.tip: For Kickham, give dates and detail: Mullinahone 1828, the accident, The Nation, Irish People, arrest 1865, Sally Cavanagh. In a Stephens-and-Kickham comparison, make Stephens the organiser and Kickham the writer and editor.

notes.h: Liberal reforms: Gladstone and the Irish Church Act (1869)
notes.b: After the Fenian scare, William Gladstone's first government (1868-74) set out to remove Irish grievances. The first target was the Church of Ireland, the state church of a mostly Catholic country.
points: Gladstone became prime minister in December 1868 and is reported as saying "My mission is to pacify Ireland", which is his stated aim.
The Manchester executions and Clerkenwell showed that Irish discontent could threaten Britain, which made reform politically urgent.
The Irish Church Act (1869) disestablished the Church of Ireland, ending its status as the state church, with effect from 1 January 1871. The Act was passed in 1869 but took effect only then.

The Church lost most of its endowments (property and income), which passed to a commission, while serving clergy received compensation. This removed an old grievance for Catholics and Presbyterians, who had paid for a church they did not attend.
Fenian prisoners were released in stages from 1869, with a conditional pardon for most in 1871, as the amnesty movement (the campaign for their release) grew.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level answers earn marks for correct dated facts: Gladstone's mission (December 1868), the Church Act 1869 and its effect from 1 January 1871. Don't confuse it with the 1851 Titles Act.

notes.h: Liberal reforms: the Irish Land Act (1870)
notes.b: Gladstone's second target was the land system, in which tenants had no legal security and landlords could raise rents or evict. The Land Act went some way but stopped short of real security.
points: The Irish Land Act (1870) gave legal force to the Ulster custom, the tenant's right to sell his interest to an incoming tenant. Before this the custom depended on landlords' goodwill.
It gave tenants compensation for disturbance when evicted for reasons other than non-payment of rent, and compensation for improvements they had made to the holding.
Its Bright clauses, named after John Bright, offered loans to help tenants buy their holdings, but few did.

The Act did not stop evictions for non-payment, and landlords could still raise rents, so it failed to give security of tenure. A landlord could in effect evict by demanding more rent than the tenant could pay.
Isaac Butt founded the Home Government Association in 1870, the next constitutional step, as nationalists looked to self-government by peaceful means.
notes.tip: When asked for the limits of the Land Act, name them: evictions for non-payment of rent were still allowed and rents could rise, so tenants gained no real security.

notes.b: Judgements turn on whether Fenianism or constitutional reform did more to change Irish politics by 1870. Good answers state a view first and weigh the evidence on both sides.
points: Fenian achievement: it revived physical force republicanism, built a disciplined oath-bound organisation across Ireland, Britain and America, and kept the republican idea alive.

Fenian limits: it failed militarily in 1867, was heavily infiltrated by informers, split into rival groups, was condemned by the Church and had small support, so it could not threaten British rule directly.
Contemporary views: the British government saw a conspiracy; many Irish nationalists admired the martyrs; the Church saw a sinful secret society; bishops and moderate nationalists feared it.

Later views: historians argue that Fenianism, through the Manchester executions and Clerkenwell, prompted Gladstone's reforms. Its tradition lived on in the IRB, which helped organise the Easter Rising of 1916.
Liberal achievement: disestablishment ended Protestant privilege in the Church, and the Land Act gave the first legal recognition of tenants' claims.
Liberal limit: the Land Act failed to prevent eviction for non-payment, and neither measure answered demands for tenant ownership or self-government.

Overall: Fenianism or Liberal reform? Violence gave the push, but reform could not remove the grievances behind violence. Reform changed more in law, while Fenianism changed the mood and the tradition.
notes.tip: State your judgement in the first paragraph. For 'how successful was Fenianism' balance success (organisation in three countries, the Irish People, martyrs and Clerkenwell prompting reform, a legacy to 1916) against failure (crushed rising, informers, Church condemnation). Link the two: the Fenian scare made reform urgent.

Hostility between religious communities, here shown in Orange marches, Dolly's Brae and the reaction to the Ecclesiastical Titles Act.
The secret oath-bound society founded in Dublin on 17 March 1858 by James Stephens to establish an Irish republic.
The American sister organisation founded by John O'Mahony in 1858, which raised money and men for the cause.
The Fenian newspaper founded in Dublin in 1863 and suppressed in September 1865.
Allen, Larkin and O'Brien, hanged in November 1867 after a police sergeant was killed in the rescue of two Fenian prisoners.
The tenant-right organisation founded in 1850 that demanded fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale.
The group of MPs elected in 1852 on a pledge of independent opposition, broken when Keogh and Sadleir took office.
The ending of the Church of Ireland's status as the state church, passed in 1869 and in effect from 1 January 1871.
The practice by which an Ulster tenant could sell his interest in a holding, legalised by the Land Act of 1870.
